questions.q: In this textbook, which period does the term 'medieval' simply mean when it is used for Indian history?
questions.a: The period from the 11th to the 17th centuries: the book says that, for it, 'medieval' simply means this period.
o: The period from the 11th to the 17th centuries
The period from the 5th to the 14th centuries
The period from the 13th to the 19th centuries

questions.q: From the early 11th century, invasions that reshaped India's political map came from beyond which mountains?
questions.a: The Hindu Kush mountains.

questions.q:
Match each year on the chapter's timelines (Column A) with its event (Column B).
Column A: 1. 1206  2. 1347  3. 1565  4. 1671
Column B: P. Battle of Talikota and destruction of Vijayanagara city  Q. Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate  R. Battle of Saraighat, in which the Ahoms defeat the Mughals  S. Establishment of the Bahmani Sultanate
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R: 1206 is the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, 1347 the establishment of the Bahmani Sultanate, 1565 the Battle of Talikota and 1671 the Battle of Saraighat.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In this book, the term 'medieval' simply means the period from the 11th to the 17th centuries of Indian history.
Reason (R): Europe's medieval period was once thought to mark a dark age before the development of modern science.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the book uses 'medieval' only as a borrowed label for the 11th to 17th centuries because Europe's and India's histories are very different; the old 'dark age' view of Europe does not explain the dates the book chose.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'medieval' literally mean? (b) To which region's history was the term originally applied?
questions.a: (a) 'Between two ages'. (b) European history, roughly from the fall of the Roman Empire in the 5th century CE to the Renaissance.
s: (a) 'Between two ages'
(b) European history (from the fall of the Roman Empire to the Renaissance)

questions.q: The chapter's two timelines list events in these years: 1206, 1326, 1336, 1347, 1398, 1498, 1526, 1556, 1565, 1576, 1671, 1699, 1754 and 1799. Ira says, 'Every event on these timelines falls inside what this book calls the medieval period.' Test her claim: say how many of the years fall inside that period, name the events that fall outside it, and give your verdict.
questions.a: The claim is not correct. The book's medieval period is the 11th to the 17th centuries, that is, up to the year 1700. Twelve of the fourteen years (1206 to 1699) fall inside it; 1699, the formation of the Khalsa, is still in the 17th century. Two fall outside it, in the 18th century: 1754, the beginning of Maratha control of Delhi, and 1799, the establishment of the Sikh Empire. So most, but not every, event is medieval in the book's sense.
s: States the book's medieval period: the 11th to the 17th centuries (up to 1700)
Counts 12 of the 14 years inside it (1206 to 1699)
Names 1754 (Maratha control of Delhi begins) and 1799 (Sikh Empire established) as 18th-century events and rejects the claim

questions.q: Kunal reads that many invaders of this period were 'Turkic' and writes in his notes: 'Turkic means people from the country of Turkey.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: Turkic refers to peoples, languages and cultures historically associated with a vast region stretching across Central Asia all the way to Turkey and Siberia, so it does not mean people from Turkey alone.
o: Turkic refers to peoples, languages and cultures of a vast region from Central Asia to Turkey and Siberia
Turkic refers only to the rulers of the Mamluk or 'Slave' dynasty, the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate
Turkic is only another spelling of 'Tughlaq', caused by the difficulty of transcribing the Persian script
Turkic refers to the peoples who lived beyond the Aravalli hills, in the deserts of western Rajasthan

questions.q: Timur, a Turkic-Mongol conqueror from Central Asia, launched a devastating attack on Delhi at the end of which century?
questions.a: The 14th century (the chapter's timeline dates the attack to 1398).

questions.q: The chapter says that almost two sultans out of three seized power by eliminating their predecessor. If an illustrative list of Delhi sultans had 30 names, about how many of them would have come to the throne WITHOUT eliminating their predecessor?
questions.a: About 10: two out of three of 30 is 20 sultans who eliminated their predecessor, so 30 - 20 = 10 came to the throne without doing so.

questions.q: True or False: Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad and kept it there for the rest of his reign. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. A few years after the move, as his plan misfired, he shifted the capital back to Delhi.
s: States False
Reason: a few years later, as the plan misfired, he shifted the capital back to Delhi

questions.q: (a) What is meant by iconoclasm? (b) The chapter deliberately uses the word 'image' rather than 'idol' or 'icon' for sacred figures in temples. Give its reason.
questions.a: (a) Iconoclasm is the rejection or destruction of icons or religious images considered idolatrous. (b) 'Idol' and 'icon' are considered pejorative in the context of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, whose orthodox sects condemn idolatry, whereas 'image' is a neutral term in English.
s: (a) Rejection or destruction of icons or religious images considered idolatrous
(b) 'Idol' and 'icon' are pejorative in the context of Judaism, Christianity and Islam; 'image' is neutral

questions.q: Answer briefly about the Delhi Sultanate. (a) After the defeat of which king in 1192 was it formed? (b) Name the first and the last of its five dynasties. (c) Of what origin were these five dynasties?
questions.a: (a) King Prithviraj Chauhan. (b) The Mamluks (the 'Slave dynasty') first and the Lodis last. (c) Turkic-Afghan origin.
s: (a) Prithviraj Chauhan
(b) Mamluks (Slave dynasty) first, Lodis last
(c) Turkic-Afghan

questions.q:
Read this illustrative scene. In a Delhi market in the 1330s, Hasan sells a bale of cloth for 10 silver coins. A royal order now says that certain cheap coins must be accepted as if they had the value of silver or gold coins. A buyer offers Hasan 10 of the new cheap coins instead of 10 silver ones. Hasan notices that the metal-worker next door can cast pieces that look exactly like the new coins at a tiny fraction of their declared value. Within months many traders refuse the new coins and prices in the market become confused.
(a) Which sultan issued this order, and what is the scheme called?
(b) Explain why the metal-worker's copies were a problem for the whole market.
(c) Why does the chapter still call the scheme a progressive idea?
(d) Using the scene and the chapter, judge whether the scheme failed because the idea itself was wrong or because of how and when it was carried out.
questions.a: (a) Muhammad bin Tughlaq; the scheme was 'token currency', in which cheap copper coins were declared to be tokens with the value of silver or gold coins. (b) Because the copper coins were cheap to make, people could counterfeit them; counterfeit coins spread, which created confusion in trade and helped make the economy decline. (c) Most of our currency today is actually 'token' currency, so the idea of a coin whose value is declared rather than contained in its metal was ahead of its time. (d) It failed in the way it was carried out: the chapter says his ambitious schemes were often poorly executed, and at that time the token coins created confusion and encouraged counterfeiting, even though the idea itself is the basis of today's currency.
s: (a) Muhammad bin Tughlaq; token currency
(b) Cheap copper coins were easy to counterfeit, so trade became confused and the economy declined
(c) Most of today's currency is token currency
(d) Judges that execution, not the idea, failed: poorly executed scheme that caused confusion and counterfeiting at the time

questions.q: A temple-town guidebook says: 'Malik Kafur's army certainly attacked Srirangam, Madurai, Chidambaram and Rameswaram.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter names Srirangam, Madurai and Chidambaram among the Hindu centres Malik Kafur attacked, but says only that Rameswaram was possibly attacked.
o: It names Srirangam, Madurai and Chidambaram, but says only 'possibly' Rameswaram
It says these southern attacks were led by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and not by Malik Kafur
It says Malik Kafur's army attacked only Warangal and Daulatabad, not these centres
It says Malik Kafur's army turned back without going south of the Deccan

questions.q: A documentary says: 'The Delhi Sultanate was a strong, stable state that collapsed suddenly at Panipat in 1526.' Evaluate this statement. (a) State what the First Battle of Panipat did to the Sultanate. (b), (c) and (d) Give three different kinds of evidence from the chapter that the Sultanate had been unstable or shrinking long before 1526. (e) Give your overall verdict on the statement.
questions.a: (a) At Panipat in 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, and that defeat put a final end to the Delhi Sultanate. (b) Unstable successions: almost two sultans out of three seized power by eliminating their predecessor, so the average reign was hardly more than nine years. (c) Failed schemes and short-lived dominance: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rule over most of the Subcontinent did not last, and his capital shift and token currency misfired, the second making the economy decline. (d) Resistance and loss of territory: kingdoms such as the Eastern Gangas were never subdued, regional sultanates such as the Bahmani broke away, and after Timur's attack at the end of the 14th century left Delhi in ruins, the Lodis ruled a Sultanate whose territory had shrunk considerably. (e) The statement is only partly right: 1526 was the final end, but it was not the sudden fall of a strong, stable state; it was the last blow to a Sultanate that had been unstable and shrinking for a long time.
s: (a) Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, which finally ended the Sultanate
One kind of evidence: violent successions (two of three sultans eliminated their predecessor; reigns of about nine years)
A second kind: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's short-lived dominance and failed schemes (capital shift, token currency)
A third kind: resistance and breakaway sultanates, or Timur's attack leaving the Lodi Sultanate much shrunk
Verdict: partly right; 1526 was the end, but the decline was long, not sudden

questions.q: Which ruler of the Eastern Ganga kingdom built the famed Surya temple at Konark, partly to commemorate his victories over the Delhi Sultanate?
questions.a: Narasimhadeva I (also spelt Narasingha Deva I), the mid-13th century Eastern Ganga ruler.

questions.q: (a) According to Kannada folklore, how did the Hoysala dynasty get its name? (b) Name one place where the Hoysalas built magnificent temples.
questions.a: (a) A young man named Sala fought a lion to save his guru, and the cry 'Hoy (strike)! Sala' gave the dynasty its name. (b) Belur or Halebidu.
s: (a) Sala fought a lion to save his guru: 'Hoy (strike)! Sala'
(b) Belur or Halebidu

questions.q: True or False: The Delhi Sultanate failed to subdue the Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga, which included present-day Odisha and parts of Bengal and Andhra Pradesh. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. Many kingdoms fell to the Sultanate, but it failed to subdue Kalinga: its mid-13th century ruler Narasimhadeva I repelled multiple inroads of the Sultanate and even defeated the Sultanate's governor of Bengal.
s: States True
Reason: Narasimhadeva I repelled multiple Sultanate inroads and defeated its governor of Bengal

questions.q:
Consider these statements about powers that resisted the Delhi Sultanate.
I. The Hoysalas ruled parts of southern India, mostly present-day Karnataka.
II. Rana Kumbha, who offered stiff resistance in the 15th century, was the ruler of the Marwar kingdom.
III. The Bahmani Sultanate rose in the mid-14th century and controlled much of the Deccan for a while.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only: statement II is wrong because Rana Kumbha was the ruler of the Mewar kingdom, not Marwar.

questions.q: Each clue below describes a power that checked the Delhi Sultanate in a different region. Name the power in each case. (a) East: the kingdom of Kalinga, which the Sultanate never subdued. (b) Present-day Telangana: Telugu chieftains who rallied over 75 more chieftains and expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq's army from Warangal. (c) South: the only independent kingdom left in the south after fending off several attacks. (d) Deccan: an independent sultanate that rose in the mid-14th century. (e) Rajasthan: the 15th-century ruler of Mewar who also repelled invasions from the later sultanates.
questions.a: (a) The Eastern Gangas (the Eastern Ganga kingdom). (b) The Musunuri Nayakas. (c) The Hoysalas. (d) The Bahmani Sultanate. (e) Rana Kumbha.
s: (a) Eastern Gangas
(b) Musunuri Nayakas
(c) Hoysalas
(d) Bahmani Sultanate
(e) Rana Kumbha

questions.q: Arjun writes: 'The Musunuri Nayakas and their confederacy drove Ala-ud-din Khilji's army out of Warangal.' Show, using the chapter, that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter places the Musunuri Nayakas' victory in the time of the Tughlaqs, around 1330-1336, and says the army they expelled from Warangal was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's. In the Sultanate's line of dynasties the Khiljis came before the Tughlaqs: Ala-ud-din Khilji campaigned at the turn of the 14th century, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled Delhi a few decades later. So by 1330-1336 the Khiljis no longer ruled Delhi, and the army driven out could not have been Ala-ud-din's.
s: Dates the Musunuri victory to the Tughlaqs' time, around 1330-1336, against Muhammad bin Tughlaq's army
Places the Khiljis before the Tughlaqs: Ala-ud-din at the turn of the 14th century, Muhammad bin Tughlaq a few decades later
Concludes that the Khiljis no longer ruled by 1330-1336, so the army was not Ala-ud-din's

questions.q: A guide at Hampi tells visitors: 'Krishnadevaraya founded this empire after he rejected the authority of Delhi.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The kingdom that grew into the Vijayanagara Empire was founded by the brothers Harihara and Bukka Raya, who had served as governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq before rejecting Delhi's authority; Krishnadevaraya ruled later, at its 16th-century peak.
o: It was founded by Harihara and Bukka Raya, who had been governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq
It was founded by Ramaraya, who rejected Delhi's authority after defeating the Deccan Sultanates
It was founded by the Hoysala kings, who moved south after breaking away from the Delhi Sultanate
It was founded by Vidyaranya, a governor who had served under Ala-ud-din Khilji in the Deccan

questions.q: Krishnadevaraya himself composed an epic poem in Telugu on the story of the Tamil poet-saint Andal. What is this work called?
questions.a: Amuktamalyada; the Rajaniti ('royal policy') is only one section of it.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Portuguese travellers who came to Vijayanagara were very well treated.
Reason (R): They came to sell horses, and the king did not want them to go and sell those precious horses to enemy kingdoms.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the Portuguese were treated well precisely because the king wanted their horses for himself and not for his enemies.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) In which present-day state is Hampi, the site of the Vijayanagara capital? (b) Name the temple in the capital whose great hall has 'musical pillars' that give out different notes when struck.
questions.a: (a) Karnataka. (b) The Vitthala temple.
s: (a) Karnataka
(b) Vitthala temple

questions.q: 'Pati' means 'lord' or 'master' and was used in the titles of many ruling dynasties of this period. According to the chapter, which rulers carried each of these titles? (a) Narapati (b) Ashwapati (c) Gajapati
questions.a: (a) The Vijayanagara kings. (b) The rulers of the Bahmani Sultanate. (c) The Gajapati rulers of Odisha, in the east, with whom Vijayanagara fought.
s: (a) Vijayanagara kings
(b) Bahmani Sultanate rulers
(c) Rulers of Odisha

questions.q: A student's essay says that Krishnadevaraya led the Vijayanagara forces at the Battle of Talikota in 1565. Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: Krishnadevaraya had died of illness in 1529; at Talikota the Vijayanagara forces were led by Ramaraya, his son-in-law.
o: He had died of illness in 1529; Ramaraya, his son-in-law, led the forces
He was away fighting the Gajapati rulers; the forces at Talikota were led by Bukka Raya
He had been killed at Panipat in 1526; the forces at Talikota were led by the Nayakas
He had retired to Tirupati as a pilgrim; the forces at Talikota were led by Harihara

questions.q: Meghna says: 'Krishnadevaraya's support for culture was limited to the Telugu language and to his own capital.' Test her claim with evidence from the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: The claim is not correct. He patronised poets and scholars in Sanskrit, Telugu and Kannada, not Telugu alone. His own Telugu epic, Amuktamalyada, tells the story of Andal, a Tamil poet-saint, so even his Telugu work drew on a Tamil tradition. He gave grants to temples beyond his capital, such as Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh, as well as to the Vitthala temple in Vijayanagara. Verdict: his patronage reached well beyond Telugu and beyond the capital.
s: Patronised poets and scholars in Sanskrit, Telugu and Kannada, not Telugu alone
His Telugu epic Amuktamalyada tells the story of the Tamil poet-saint Andal
Grants to Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh as well as the Vitthala temple in the capital; claim rejected

questions.q: A quiz card reads: 'Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 mainly with war elephants and cavalry charges.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The battle relied heavily on gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns, which had recently been introduced in warfare in India.
o: It relied heavily on gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns
It relied on guerrilla attacks by Bhil archers who knew the paths of the Aravalli hills
It relied on a large fleet of river boats and soldiers expert at rowing them
It relied on troops supplied by mansabdars, each keeping a set number of horses

questions.q: Which of these actions of Akbar best fits the doctrine of sulh-i-kul that he promoted?
questions.a: Holding dialogues with scholars of different faiths: sulh-i-kul means 'peace with all' or tolerance of all faiths, and Akbar pursued it through interfaith dialogues.
o: Holding dialogues at his court with scholars of different faiths
Besieging the Rajput fort of Chittor for more than five months
Reimposing a pilgrimage tax on Hindus travelling to sacred places
Declaring cheap copper coins to have the value of silver ones

questions.q: True or False: Akbar's reign lasted almost 50 years, from 1556 to his death in 1605. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. 1605 - 1556 = 49 years, and the chapter describes his long reign as lasting almost 50 years, from 1556 to his death in 1605.
s: States True
Reason: 1605 - 1556 = 49, which the chapter calls almost 50 years

questions.q: (a) Which Sanskrit epic was translated into Persian as the Razmnama at Akbar's house of translation? (b) What does the name 'Razmnama' mean?
questions.a: (a) The Mahabharata. (b) The 'Book of War'.
s: (a) The Mahabharata
(b) 'Book of War'

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the Mughals.
I. Shah Jahan was Akbar's son and tried to expand the empire into the Deccan.
II. Babur turned his sights to India after he had been thrown out of Samarkand, in present-day Uzbekistan.
III. Akbar besieged the fort of Chittor for more than five months before it was breached.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only: statement I is wrong because it was Jahangir who was Akbar's son and tried to expand the empire into the Deccan; Shah Jahan was Jahangir's son.

questions.q: A class quiz board on the Mughals has five cards. Write the one answer each card asks for. (a) Babur: the name of his memoirs. (b) Akbar: his age when he was declared emperor. (c) Akbar: the city where he set up a 'house of translation'. (d) Jahangir: what he shared with his father Akbar. (e) Shah Jahan: the monument at Agra he is best remembered for building.
questions.a: (a) The Baburnama ('Babur's Memoirs'). (b) 13. (c) Fatehpur Sikri. (d) A love for art and architecture. (e) The Taj Mahal.
s: (a) Baburnama
(b) 13 years
(c) Fatehpur Sikri
(d) Love for art and architecture
(e) Taj Mahal

questions.q: Dev says: 'From Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526, Delhi stayed under Mughal rule without a break.' Test his claim using what the chapter says happened after Babur's death in 1530, and give your verdict.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. After Babur's death Humayun struggled to hold the empire together, and Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan leader, set up the Sur Empire over large parts of north India. Himu, the chief minister of one of the last Suri rulers, then captured Delhi and ruled it briefly as Hemchandra Vikramaditya. Only after Akbar defeated Himu at the Second Battle of Panipat did Akbar reclaim Delhi for the Mughals. So Mughal rule over Delhi was broken.
s: Humayun lost large parts of north India to Sher Shah Suri's Sur Empire
Himu captured Delhi and ruled it briefly as Hemchandra Vikramaditya
Akbar reclaimed Delhi only after the Second Battle of Panipat; the claim is rejected

questions.q: When Aurangzeb crowned himself emperor in 1658, he named himself 'Alamgir'. What does this title mean?
questions.a: 'Conqueror of the world'.

questions.q: Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 until his death in 1707. Which of these events from the chapter took place during his reign?
questions.a: The Battle of Saraighat, fought in 1671, when Aurangzeb had sent Mughal forces against the Ahoms; Haldighati (1576) and the Second Battle of Panipat (1556) came before his reign, and the Sikh Empire (1799) after it.
o: The Battle of Saraighat, in which the Ahoms defeated the Mughals
The Battle of Haldighati, in which Maharana Pratap was forced to retreat
The Second Battle of Panipat, Akbar's decisive victory
The establishment of the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mughal power grew stronger in the years right after Aurangzeb's death in 1707.
Reason (R): Maintaining large armies for Aurangzeb's long wars in the Deccan depleted the empire's treasury.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: the chapter speaks of the rapid decline of Mughal power after Aurangzeb's death, and the drain of the Deccan wars on the treasury and the administration is often considered one of the key factors in that decline.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: (a) Name the two taxes that Aurangzeb reimposed. (b) Which earlier Mughal emperor had abolished both of them?
questions.a: (a) The jizya on non-Muslims, and a pilgrimage tax on Hindus travelling to their sacred places. (b) Akbar.
s: (a) Jizya on non-Muslims and pilgrimage tax on Hindus
(b) Akbar

questions.q: (a) What is a farman? (b) What did Aurangzeb's farman of 1669 order the governors of all provinces to do? (c) Name two places where, according to the chapter, temples were destroyed.
questions.a: (a) A farman (or firman) is an edict, an order issued by the ruler. (b) To demolish the schools and temples of the 'infidels' and put down their teachings and religious practices. (c) Any two of Banaras (present-day Varanasi), Mathura and Somnath.
s: (a) An edict
(b) Demolish schools and temples of the 'infidels' and put down their teachings and practices
(c) Any two of Banaras (Varanasi), Mathura, Somnath

questions.q: True or False: Because the Mughal Empire reached its greatest expansion under Aurangzeb, his reign was free of major rebellions. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. The empire did reach its greatest expansion under him, but he was constantly faced with significant rebellions and spent the last 25 years of his life fighting war after war in the Deccan.
s: States False
Reason: despite the greatest expansion he constantly faced significant rebellions and fought in the Deccan for his last 25 years

questions.q: An essay says: 'Aurangzeb won the throne, enlarged the empire and handed it on in strong shape.' Check each of the three parts of this sentence against the chapter and give an overall verdict.
questions.a: Part 1 is right: he defeated and executed Dara Shikoh, removed his other two brothers, imprisoned Shah Jahan in the Agra Fort and crowned himself in 1658. Part 2 is right: under him the Mughal Empire reached its greatest expansion, with conquests in the South in particular. Part 3 is wrong: the long Deccan wars depleted the treasury and strained the administration, and Mughal power declined rapidly after his death in 1707; even his own last letters say 'of the future there is no hope'. Verdict: the sentence is partly right.
s: Part 1 right: defeated his brothers, imprisoned Shah Jahan, crowned himself in 1658
Part 2 right: the empire reached its greatest expansion under him
Part 3 wrong: treasury depleted, rapid decline after 1707; verdict partly right

questions.q: Who was the Ahom military commander at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671?
questions.a: Lachit Borphukan, who with 10,000 men defeated a Mughal force of 30,000 soldiers.

questions.q:
Match each resister of Mughal power (Column A) with the region or kingdom the chapter links to it (Column B).
Column A: 1. The Jat peasantry  2. Rani Durgavati  3. Durga Das Rathore  4. The Ahoms
Column B: P. The Garha kingdom, a Gond kingdom in central India  Q. The Brahmaputra Valley  R. Present-day western Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and eastern Rajasthan  S. Marwar, fighting to protect the independence of Jodhpur
questions.a: 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q: the Jats were in present-day western Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and eastern Rajasthan; Rani Durgavati ruled the Garha kingdom; Durga Das Rathore of Marwar fought for Jodhpur; the Ahoms formed their kingdom in the Brahmaputra Valley.

questions.q:
A Class 8 heritage club is making a poster about a queen of one of the Gond kingdoms of central India. Their notes read: 'She ruled wisely and made her kingdom prosperous. She kept an army of 20,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants and repelled several attempted invasions. In 1564 a general sent by the Mughal emperor attacked her kingdom. Outnumbered and outmatched in weaponry, she led her troops herself.'
(a) Name the queen and her kingdom.
(b) How many soldiers did she keep for every elephant?
(c) Which Mughal emperor sent the general who attacked her in 1564?
(d) Name two tribal groups other than the Gonds that, according to the chapter, also fought back against attempts to annex their territory or tax them.
questions.a: (a) Rani Durgavati of the Garha kingdom. (b) 20,000 / 1,000 = 20 soldiers for every elephant. (c) Akbar. (d) Any two of the Bhils, the Santhals and the Kochs.
s: (a) Rani Durgavati, Garha kingdom
(b) 20 soldiers per elephant (20,000 / 1,000)
(c) Akbar
(d) Any two of the Bhils, Santhals, Kochs

questions.q: (a) From which present-day country did the Ahoms migrate in the 13th century? (b) In which river valley did they form the Ahom kingdom?
questions.a: (a) Myanmar. (b) The Brahmaputra Valley.
s: (a) Myanmar
(b) Brahmaputra Valley

questions.q: At a folk performance in Rajasthan, a singer tells ballads of Rajput heroes. A listener asks: 'Why were the Rajputs so often fighting invaders, and did they ever unite against them?' Answer the listener from the chapter in four points: (a) one reason linked to their location, (b) one reason linked to their traditions, (c) the two major clans that emerged when they rebuilt their kingdoms after the Khiljis' conquest, and (d) the ruler who unified several clans, and how his struggle ended.
questions.a: (a) Their location in northwest India put them in the path of invading forces from beyond the Subcontinent. (b) They inherited proud traditions from earlier dynasties such as the Pratiharas, who had resisted the Arab invasions of Sindh. (c) The clans of Mewar and Marwar. (d) Rana Sanga, in the early 16th century, unified several Rajput clans and won many battles against sultans, but was finally defeated by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa.
s: (a) Location in northwest India, in the path of invaders
(b) Proud traditions inherited from dynasties such as the Pratiharas, who resisted the Arab invasions of Sindh
(c) Mewar and Marwar
(d) Rana Sanga unified several clans but was defeated by Babur at Khanwa

questions.q: Rohan says: 'Against the Mughals, numbers decided everything: a rebel force with enough fighters could win, and a small force never could.' Evaluate his claim. (a) Give the strength of each side at the Battle of Saraighat (1671) and the result. (b) Give the number of Jat fighters who confronted the Mughal army in the 17th century, and the result. (c) Compare the Jat and the Ahom numbers: what does the comparison show about Rohan's claim? (d) Name two things the chapter says the Ahoms used to repulse a larger Mughal force, and one other resister who fought in a similar way. (e) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) Lachit Borphukan's 10,000 Ahom men defeated a Mughal force of 30,000 soldiers. (b) 20,000 Jats fought valiantly, but their leader was killed and the rebellion was suppressed. (c) The Jats had twice as many fighters as the Ahoms (20,000 against 10,000), yet the Jats lost while the smaller Ahom force won, so the number of fighters alone did not decide the result. (d) Their knowledge of the terrain (dense forests, hills and rivers) and persistent guerrilla tactics; Maharana Pratap also waged guerrilla warfare from the Aravalli hills, helped by Bhils who knew the terrain. (e) The claim is rejected: a small force could beat a much larger one, and a large rebel force could still lose; knowledge of the terrain and tactics mattered as much as numbers.
s: (a) 10,000 Ahoms under Lachit Borphukan defeated 30,000 Mughals
(b) 20,000 Jats; leader killed, rebellion suppressed
(c) Jats had twice the Ahom number yet lost, so numbers alone did not decide
(d) Knowledge of terrain and guerrilla tactics; Maharana Pratap (with the Bhils) as a similar case
(e) Verdict: claim rejected; terrain and tactics mattered as much as numbers

questions.q: In 15th-century Punjab, Guru Nanak spread a message that included Ik Onkar. What does Ik Onkar stand for?

questions.q: True or False: The Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, marks the site where Guru Gobind Singh was beheaded. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. It marks the site where Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was beheaded on Aurangzeb's orders in 1675; Guru Gobind Singh was his son, the tenth Guru, who went on to establish the Khalsa.

questions.a: (a) Any two of truthfulness, compassion, humility and self-control. (b) '... truthful living.'

(b) Truthful living

questions.q: For each event below, write the Sikh response that followed it, according to the chapter. (a) Emperor Jahangir had Guru Arjan tortured to death. (b) In 1675 a group of Kashmiri Pandits approached Guru Tegh Bahadur seeking protection from religious persecution. (c) Guru Tegh Bahadur was publicly beheaded in Chandni Chowk on Aurangzeb's orders.

(b) Guru Tegh Bahadur stood with them and refused to convert despite torture
(c) Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the Sikhs in this chapter.
I. The Guru Granth Sahib was first compiled by Guru Arjan, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns were added later.
II. Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth and last Sikh Guru.
III. Maharaja Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh confederacies at the turn of the 18th century, soon after the Khalsa was formed.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only: statement III is wrong because Maharaja Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh confederacies at the turn of the 19th century, as Mughal power declined, not at the turn of the 18th century.

questions.q: Into how many provinces (subahs) was Akbar's empire divided, with ministers assigned to each?
questions.a: Twelve provinces (subahs).

questions.q: (a) Name the two coins of the Mughal currency system mentioned in the chapter. (b) Of which metal was each made?
questions.a: (a) The rupaya and the dam. (b) The rupaya was of silver and the dam of copper.

(b) Rupaya of silver, dam of copper

questions.q:
Read this illustrative inspection report from Akbar's time. An officer holds a rank that requires him to maintain 400 horses, 30 elephants and 50 camels, along with troops, for the state. He is paid not in coin but with the income of an assigned piece of land. At this year's inspection the officials count 340 horses, 30 elephants and 35 camels.
(a) What is such an officer called, and what is the land he is paid with called?
(b) By how many horses and how many camels is he short, and what percentage of the required horses does he actually keep?
(c) Why did the state carry out such regular inspections?
(d) The emperor needs a large army at short notice for a sudden campaign. Explain how this system lets him raise it without keeping a permanent centralised army.
questions.a: (a) A mansabdar (an officer holding a mansab, or rank); the land is a jagir, so he is also called a jagirdar. (b) 400 - 340 = 60 horses short and 50 - 35 = 15 camels short; 340 / 400 = 85% of the required horses. (c) To ensure compliance, that is, to check that each mansabdar really kept the precise number of animals and troops his rank required, as this officer has not. (d) Every mansabdar keeps a fixed number of troops and animals for the state, so the emperor only has to call the mansabdars together to assemble an army quickly; he need not pay and keep a permanent centralised army all year.
s: (a) Mansabdar; jagir (hence jagirdar)
(b) 60 horses and 15 camels short; 85% of the horses
(c) Inspections ensured compliance with the numbers each rank required
(d) Mansabdars' fixed contingents could be called together at short notice, so no permanent centralised army was needed

questions.q: A district museum shows three objects side by side: a Persian wheel, a Vijayanagara land grant inscribed on a copper plate, and a hundi. Write a museum label in four points: (a) what the Persian wheel was used for, and what the expansion of irrigation made possible; (b) what the copper-plate land grant was the equivalent of today; (c) what a hundi was and how it helped merchants; (d) what the three objects together show about India's economy in this period, according to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) It drew water from wells or tanks to irrigate fields; the expansion of irrigation increased agricultural productivity and allowed many crops, food and non-food, to be produced. (b) Modern-day property deeds. (c) A written instruction to make payment to an individual, which could be carried across political borders, so merchants could transfer funds without carrying currency and were less vulnerable to plunder. (d) That despite shifting political powers, India's economy stayed vibrant, resting on agriculture, recorded land rights and systems of credit that worked across political boundaries, so the Subcontinent remained one of the wealthiest regions in the world.
s: (a) Lifted water from wells or tanks for irrigation; irrigation raised productivity and allowed multiple crops
(b) Equivalent of modern-day property deeds
(c) Written payment instruction carried across borders; funds moved without carrying currency, safer from plunder
(d) Economy stayed vibrant despite political change; India remained one of the wealthiest regions

questions.q: An illustrative register of 150 senior officials in Akbar's administration lists 42 non-Muslims. Of the remaining 108 Muslim officials, 70 are of foreign origin and 38 of Indian origin. (a) What percentage of the 150 officials are non-Muslims? (b) Does this fit what the chapter says about the share of non-Muslim officials? Explain. (c) What percentage of the Muslim officials are of foreign origin, and does this fit the chapter? (d) The chapter says non-Muslims were kept in a minority 'despite Akbar's growing tolerance for different faiths'. What does the word 'despite' tell you? (e) A student says: 'Because Akbar was tolerant, his officials were drawn equally from every faith and origin.' Judge this claim using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 42 / 150 = 28%. (b) Yes: the chapter says the share of non-Muslim officials rarely exceeded one-third (about 33%) and was often much less, and 28% is below one-third. (c) 70 / 108 = about 65% (64.8%); this fits the chapter, which says Muslim officials of foreign origin were generally favoured over those of Indian origin. (d) That his tolerance did not translate into equal shares of high posts: tolerance and a non-Muslim minority among officials existed side by side. (e) The claim is rejected: Akbar's tolerance was real, but non-Muslims were a minority (28%, not an equal share) and foreign-origin Muslims outnumbered Indian-origin Muslims by 70 to 38.
s: (b) Fits: below the one-third the chapter says was rarely exceeded
(c) 70 / 108 = about 65%; fits the favouring of foreign-origin officials
(d) 'Despite' shows tolerance did not mean equal shares of high posts
(e) Claim rejected using the 28% and 70 to 38 figures

questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the army could be assembled quickly because each mansabdar had to maintain a precise number of troops and animals for the state; how he was paid does not explain that.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
